adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Default/Elytron/FIPS all return order() 200, so the stable sort resolves ties by ServiceLoader/classpath order and silently picks one (logged only at debug) where the old code failed fast, e.g. selecting non-FIPS DefaultCryptoProvider when both default and fips1402 jars are present

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to sort providers by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and no longer throws when multiple providers are present. In the same diff, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all implement order() and each returns 200. With equal order values, the sorted stream will not deterministically prefer FIPS over Default/Elytron; it will effectively fall back to ServiceLoader encounter/classpath order and silently choose foundProviders.get(0), only logging the others at debug. This is a behavior change from the previous fail-fast logic and can result in selecting the wrong provider when multiple 200-order providers are on the classpath.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:56 — The round-trip test only compares decoder output with itself and never verifies the signature with keyPair.getPublic() or checks the DER against the original, so encoder bugs the lax decoder accepts (wrong tag or constructed bit, bad lengths) or silently truncated r/s still pass

adjudication.rationale: In ECDSAAlgorithmTest, the assertion only checks rsConcat == rsConcat2 after decode→encode→decode using the same ASN1Decoder/ASN1Encoder (lines around `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign, ...)`, `concatenatedRSToASN1DER(...)`, then decode again). It never verifies that the re-encoded DER (`asn1Des`) matches the original DER signature (`sign`) nor does it verify the signature with `keyPair.getPublic()`. That means certain encoder defects could be masked if the decoder accepts them, making this a test-quality gap rather than a functional defect shown by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — One default-curve EC key is used for ES256/ES384/ES512 (the JDK 19+ default is P-384), so testES256 truncates 48-byte r/s to 32 bytes and produces a corrupt signature that still passes the self-consistency assert

adjudication.rationale: In ECDSAAlgorithmTest, a single EC KeyPair is generated once via KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and reused for ES256/ES384/ES512. The test’s assertion only checks that DER -> concat -> DER -> concat yields the same concatenated value, not that the reconstructed DER signature matches the original or verifies with the public key. If the generated key’s curve size doesn’t match algorithm.getSignatureLength() (e.g., ES256 expects 32-byte r/s but the key is larger), integerToBytes(...) will truncate/pad to the requested length, and the self-consistency assert can still pass while producing a DER signature that would not correspond to the original signature. This is a real, diff-grounded test weakness, but it’s not a proven production defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:153 — integerToBytes silently drops the high-order bytes when r/s is wider than signLength/2 instead of throwing, so a curve/algorithm mismatch yields an invalid JWS signature and distinct DER signatures collide to the same R||S

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider's ECDSACryptoProvider, integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength) truncates when s.toByteArray().length > qLength by copying only the last qLength bytes. This will silently discard high-order (most significant) bytes, not just an optional leading 0x00 sign byte, and can therefore produce an incorrect fixed-width R||S value if the DER INTEGER is wider than expected (e.g., curve/algorithm/signLength mismatch or malformed input). That also implies distinct DER encodings with different high-order bytes could map to the same truncated R||S output, as the finding states. This behavior is introduced in the new provider implementation in the diff and is a correctness/security issue rather than a mere style concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:94 — The decoder accepts non-DER input without error: tags are masked to 5 bits (0x10, 0xB0, 0x82 accepted as SEQUENCE/INTEGER), readSequence lets elements overrun the declared length (line 57), trailing bytes are ignored, and negative INTEGERs are accepted, e.g. r=-1 becomes 0x..FF

adjudication.rationale: The new ASN1Decoder is not a strict DER decoder and will accept malformed/non-DER inputs in ways described. In readSequence()/readInteger() it validates only the low 5-bit tag number via readTagNumber(tag) (tag & 0x1f), so tags like 0xB0 (low bits 0x10) and 0x82 (low bits 0x02) would be treated as SEQUENCE/INTEGER even though the class/constructed bits differ. In readSequence(), the loop subtracts bytes.length but never checks that readNext()’s returned element length fits within the remaining declared sequence length, so an element can overrun the declared length and still be returned (length can go negative and the loop stops after over-reading). It also does not verify that all input bytes were consumed (trailing bytes are ignored). Finally, readInteger() uses new BigInteger(bytes) (signed) with no positivity check, so negative INTEGER values (e.g., 0xFF => -1) are accepted, which is invalid for ECDSA r/s and can lead to incorrect signature conversions in AuthzClientCryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS().

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:134 — Indefinite length 0x80 returns -1, which reaches new byte[-1] (line 170, NegativeArraySizeException), and a zero-length INTEGER reaches new BigInteger(new byte[0]) (line 73, NumberFormatException), so unchecked exceptions escape instead of IOException

adjudication.rationale: In ASN1Decoder.readLength(), a length octet of 0x80 returns -1 (indefinite length). Callers like readInteger() immediately do `byte[] bytes = read(length);` which will attempt `new byte[-1]` in read(int), causing an unchecked NegativeArraySizeException rather than an IOException. Separately, readInteger() allows `length == 0`, so `read(0)` returns `new byte[0]` and `new BigInteger(bytes)` will throw NumberFormatException for a zero-length array, again escaping as an unchecked exception instead of IOException. Both behaviors are directly implied by the added code paths in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:109 — concatenatedRSToASN1DER never checks signature.length == signLength, so on the verify path trailing bytes appended to R||S are silently ignored (malleable signature accepted) and short input throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of IOException

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider#getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the method blindly copies only the first signLength bytes (len bytes for R and len bytes for S) via System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len) and System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len) without checking signature.length == signLength. If signature is longer, trailing bytes are ignored; if shorter, System.arraycopy will throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of an IOException. This matches the finding and is a real, diff-grounded correctness/security issue.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new *abstract* method `int order()` to the public `CryptoProvider` interface (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java), which is a source/binary compatibility break for any third-party provider compiled against the previous SPI. Additionally, `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` now unconditionally sorts loaded providers via `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java), so a legacy-compiled provider on the classpath would trigger `AbstractMethodError` when `order()` is invoked during sorting. Making `order()` a `default` method (e.g., returning 0) would avoid that runtime failure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:64 — detectProvider no longer fails fast when several providers are found; because Default, FIPS1402 and Elytron all return order 200, a tie is settled silently by ServiceLoader classpath order and logged only at debug level, so a FIPS classpath that also carries crypto-default can end up on non-FIPS crypto with no error.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` from throwing an `IllegalStateException` when `foundProviders.size() > 1` to instead sorting by `CryptoProvider::order` (descending) and always returning `foundProviders.get(0)`, only logging the rest at DEBUG (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java). The diff also sets `order()` to the same value (200) for DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider, meaning ties are not deterministically resolved by the code and will fall back to ServiceLoader discovery/classpath order. adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:76 — Around 15 methods are IDE-template stubs throwing UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet."), which implies unfinished TODO work and doesn't say that the provider supports only ECDSA conversion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:134 — readLength() returns a -1 indefinite-length sentinel that no caller handles (readInteger then hits NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException), which is leftover code copied from a general-purpose parser.
matched_golden_ids: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both point to the same root problem: readLength() can return -1 to indicate indefinite-length encoding, but the rest of the decoding logic doesn’t handle that sentinel properly, leading to incorrect/unsafe length arithmetic and downstream failures (e.g., negative sizes/exceptions) instead of correct processing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:52 — Tag checks compare only the low 5 tag-number bits (class/constructed bits are ignored) and borrow constants from ASN1Encoder, so the decoder accepts non-universal tags and is coupled to the encoder.

adjudication.rationale: In ASN1Decoder.readSequence() and readInteger(), the code validates tags using readTagNumber(tag) and compares only the low 5 bits (tag & 0x1f) against ASN1Encoder.SEQUENCE/INTEGER. This ignores the tag class and constructed bit, so e.g. a context-specific tag with the same tag-number (non-universal) would be accepted as a SEQUENCE/INTEGER. Given the methods are intended to parse DER for ECDSA signatures, this is a real correctness/validation flaw exposed by the new decoder implementation. The coupling to ASN1Encoder constants is also present (decoder depends on encoder’s tag constants).

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/pom.xml:67 — The hamcrest test dependency is added but not used (ECDSAAlgorithmTest only uses org.junit.Assert).

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:672 — One default-size EC key pair is used for ES256/384/512, so P-521 (and the long-form DER length paths in ASN1Encoder.writeLength/ASN1Decoder.readLength) is never tested, and the round-trip never compares output against the JDK's DER signature.

That means ES512 does not exercise P-521-sized signatures, and consequently the >127 (long-form) length handling in `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` / `ASN1Decoder.readLength` may never be executed. Also, the test only asserts `rsConcat` round-trips (`rsConcat` == `rsConcat2`) and never asserts the re-encoded DER (`asn1Des`) matches the original JDK DER (`sign`). The cited line number (672) is incorrect for this added 74-line file, but the substance of the test-coverage concern is verifiable from the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:64 — Removing the multiple-provider failure means equal-order providers (Default/FIPS/Elytron all return 200) are picked arbitrarily by classpath order with only a debug log, so e.g. a FIPS deployment with a stray keycloak-crypto-default jar silently runs non-FIPS instead of failing fast.

In the same diff, Default/FIPS/Elytron providers all implement `order()` returning `200`, so when more than one of these is on the classpath the comparator tie leaves selection dependent on `ServiceLoader` iteration order (i.e., effectively classpath/provider-file order) with no failure. This can silently pick a non-FIPS provider in a FIPS deployment, which is a real behavior/security defect introduced by this change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java:44 — order() is added as an abstract (non-default) SPI method, so any CryptoProvider compiled against the old interface (custom or version-skewed jar) throws AbstractMethodError from the sort comparator now that authz-client always contributes a second provider to the ServiceLoader scan.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new abstract SPI method `int order()` to `CryptoProvider` (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoProvider.java) and immediately calls it during provider detection via `ServiceLoader` sorting (`CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` now does `.sorted(Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order).reversed())`). Any `CryptoProvider` implementation compiled against the previous interface (and thus lacking `order()`) will throw `AbstractMethodError` when the sort comparator invokes `order()`. adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — AuthzClient.create pins the JVM-global CryptoIntegration provider using only authz-client's classloader (first caller wins, later init(cl) calls are no-ops), so in shared/parent-classloader or TCCL-differing setups the stub AuthzClientCryptoProvider is selected even when a full provider is available to the app, and other Keycloak code then hits its UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.") stubs at runtime.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` in `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)`, forcing crypto-provider auto-detection to run using the authz-client module’s classloader. The authz-client also adds its own `CryptoProvider` via `META-INF/services/...` (`AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, order=100) whose methods largely throw `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")`. If the authz-client classloader cannot see the full-featured providers (e.g., `DefaultCryptoProvider`/FIPS/Elytron, order=200) even though they are available to the application via a different/parent/TCCL, provider detection may select the stub provider and later calls into `CryptoIntegration.getProvider()` can hit those UOE stubs at runtime. The classloader-pinning concern is grounded in the new init call and the stub provider implementation; the “first caller wins / later init no-ops” detail isn’t shown here but the risk of selecting the wrong provider due to the chosen classloader is directly introduced by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — Eager CryptoIntegration.init in create() makes ServiceLoader instantiation of every CryptoProvider on the classpath a hard prerequisite even for client-secret users, so a provider with missing deps (e.g. crypto-default without bcprov) now throws ServiceConfigurationError/NoClassDefFoundError out of AuthzClient.create.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` unconditionally in `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)`. `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` uses `ServiceLoader.load(...).spliterator()` and immediately streams/collects into a `List` (and now sorts by `order()`), which necessarily iterates and instantiates each `CryptoProvider` found. If any provider on the classpath fails to load/initialize due to missing transitive deps, that failure can surface during `AuthzClient.create(...)` even if the caller never uses crypto features (e.g., client-secret flows). This is a behavior change introduced by the diff and can break client creation at runtime.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:73 — A zero-length DER INTEGER reaches new BigInteger(new byte[0]) and throws unchecked NumberFormatException instead of the declared IOException.

adjudication.rationale: In ASN1Decoder.readInteger(), the length is taken from readLength() and then bytes are read with read(length). If the DER/BER stream encodes an INTEGER with length 0, read(0) returns an empty byte array and new BigInteger(bytes) will throw an unchecked NumberFormatException. The method declares `throws IOException` and does not guard against `length == 0`, so malformed input can cause an unexpected runtime exception instead of an IOException.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:109 — concatenatedRSToASN1DER never checks signature.length against signLength, so a short or malformed signature throws unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException rather than IOException, and an oversized one is silently truncated.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the code unconditionally does `System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len)` and `System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len)` where `len = signLength/2`. There is no check that `signature.length == signLength` (or at least `>= signLength`). If `signature` is shorter, `System.arraycopy` will throw an unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. If `signature` is longer, only the first `signLength` bytes are used and the remainder is ignored (silent truncation). The finding accurately describes behavior visible in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Removing the multiple-provider fail-fast means FIPS1402Provider, DefaultCryptoProvider and WildFlyElytronProvider (all order 200) tie, so classpath/ServiceLoader order silently decides whether FIPS or non-FIPS crypto is used, with the ignored provider logged only at debug level.

adjudication.rationale: In CryptoIntegration.detectProvider(), the ServiceLoader results are now sorted by CryptoProvider::order descending and the previous fail-fast on foundProviders.size() > 1 was removed; the code always returns foundProviders.get(0) and only logs the rest at debug. In this diff, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all implement order() as 200, so they tie. With a tie, the chosen provider depends on ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order, making selection between FIPS and non-FIPS providers nondeterministic and silent at normal log levels.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:109 — concatenatedRSToASN1DER never checks signature.length == signLength: trailing bytes on an untrusted JWS signature are ignored, so modified signatures still verify (malleability), and short ones throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of IOException.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the code blindly does System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len) and System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len) without validating signature.length == signLength. If signature is shorter than signLength this will throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (not an IOException as the method signature suggests). If signature is longer, the extra trailing bytes are ignored because only the first signLength bytes are copied into r/s, which can allow accepting modified inputs where the prefix is unchanged.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:52 — The hand-written DER decoder is not strict: it compares only the low 5 tag bits (ignores class and constructed bit), accepts indefinite length 0x80 (readInteger then throws NegativeArraySizeException at line 170), ignores trailing data after the SEQUENCE, and integerToBytes silently truncates oversized r/s instead of rejecting them.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a hand-written ASN.1/DER decoder whose behavior is demonstrably unsafe/incorrect for malformed inputs. In ASN1Decoder.readLength(), length==0x80 returns -1 (indefinite length), but callers like readInteger() immediately do read(length), which allocates `new byte[length]` and will throw NegativeArraySizeException for such input. Also, tag validation in readSequence()/readInteger() compares only `tag & 0x1f` via readTagNumber(tag), ignoring the class/constructed bits, so non-DER/incorrect tags could be accepted. Finally, readSequence() does not ensure the entire input is consumed (extra trailing bytes after the SEQUENCE are not rejected), and integerToBytes in AuthzClientCryptoProvider truncates oversized integers instead of rejecting them, potentially accepting malformed ECDSA signatures. These are concrete, diff-grounded correctness/robustness issues.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — AuthzClient.create() runs the first-caller-wins CryptoIntegration.init with the authz-client classloader. In modular deployments that classloader may not see the FIPS/default provider, so AuthzClientCryptoProvider (JDK default KeyStore provider) can get pinned JVM-wide and later init calls become no-ops.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` in `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` and also adds a service entry for `org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` pointing to `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`. This makes crypto-provider selection depend on the authz-client module/classloader at the time `AuthzClient.create()` is first called. In modular/classloader-isolated deployments, that classloader may only see `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (order=100) and not the higher-preference default/FIPS providers (order=200), so the chosen provider could be the “wrong” one for the overall runtime. However, the claim that `CryptoIntegration.init` is strictly “first-caller-wins” and becomes a JVM-wide pinned no-op on later calls is not shown in the provided diff (the `init` method behavior isn’t included), so the full failure mode can’t be verified from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/AuthzClientCryptoProvider.java:63 — getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore provider (usually SUN), not a BouncyCastle provider, so BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER silently resolves to a JDK provider for any code that depends on the BC contract.

adjudication.rationale: In the added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which will typically return the JDK keystore provider (e.g., `SUN`/`SUNJSSE`), not a BouncyCastle provider. Since `CryptoProvider#getBouncyCastleProvider()` is explicitly a BC-provider contract, returning a non-BC provider is incorrect behavior and can break any code that assumes the returned provider is actually BouncyCastle (or at least misleads consumers instead of failing fast).

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:42 — One default-curve EC key is reused for ES256/ES384/ES512; on JDK 19+ (P-384 default) ES256 r/s get silently truncated by integerToBytes, and the self-consistency assert still passes, so the test hides lossy conversion instead of using P-256/P-384/P-521 per algorithm.

adjudication.rationale: In ECDSAAlgorithmTest, a single EC KeyPair is generated once via KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() and reused for ES256/ES384/ES512. The production conversion helpers are called with algorithm-specific signature lengths (algorithm.getSignatureLength()), and integerToBytes(...) in AuthzClientCryptoProvider will truncate if the BigInteger byte array is longer than qLength. Therefore, if the generated key’s curve size is larger than the algorithm’s expected length (e.g., a 384-bit key used with ES256’s 32-byte halves), the test can still pass while exercising a lossy truncation path, making the test potentially misleading. The specific claim about JDK 19+ defaulting to P-384 isn’t verifiable from the diff, but the underlying issue (test should generate curve-matching keys per algorithm) is grounded in the code shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:56 — The assertion only checks that rsConcat == rsConcat2. It never checks that the re-encoded DER equals the original JCA signature or passes Signature.verify, so a bug that is symmetric in the encoder and decoder would go unnoticed.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` only asserts a round-trip property: it converts a valid JCA DER signature to concatenated RS (`asn1derToConcatenatedRS`), re-encodes it (`concatenatedRSToASN1DER`), then decodes again and asserts `rsConcat` equals `rsConcat2` (lines around 48-56). It does not assert that the re-encoded DER (`asn1Des`) is equivalent to the original DER signature (`sign`) or that `asn1Des` verifies with `Signature.verify`. Therefore, an encoder/decoder pair with a consistent but wrong transformation could still pass this test, which is a concrete test coverage gap introduced by this diff rather than a runtime defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:70 — testES512 never signs with a P-521 key, so DER sequences stay under 128 bytes and the long-form length paths (ASN1Encoder.writeLength, ASN1Decoder.readLength 0x81) are never run.

adjudication.rationale: The claim that the long-form length paths are never exercised is not supported by the diff. In `ECDSAAlgorithmTest.testES512`, the test calls `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign, algorithm.getSignatureLength())` and then `concatenatedRSToASN1DER(rsConcat, algorithm.getSignatureLength())`. For `ES512`, `algorithm.getSignatureLength()` is expected to be 132, making each of R and S 66 bytes. In `concatenatedRSToASN1DER`, those 66-byte halves are converted to `BigInteger`s and re-encoded as a DER SEQUENCE whose payload is typically > 127 bytes (two INTEGERs of ~66 bytes each plus overhead), which will cause `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` to use long-form length (0x81/0x82). The subsequent decode `asn1derToConcatenatedRS(asn1Des, ...)` must then parse that long-form length in `ASN1Decoder.readLength`. Therefore, even if the EC key generated is not P-521, the test still drives the long-form length code paths due to the fixed `signLength` parameter.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/util/crypto/ASN1Decoder.java:49 — The new hand-written ASN.1 decoder has no negative tests: wrong SEQUENCE/INTEGER tag, sequence size != 2, truncated input, indefinite length, out-of-bounds long-form length, and r/s larger than signLength/2 are all untested.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a hand-written ASN.1 DER encoder/decoder (ASN1Decoder/ASN1Encoder) and uses it for ECDSA signature conversions in AuthzClientCryptoProvider. The only added test (ECDSAAlgorithmTest) is a positive round-trip check; it does not cover failure/edge paths that are explicitly present in the new code, such as wrong tag handling in ASN1Decoder.readSequence/readInteger (throws on non-SEQUENCE/non-INTEGER), truncated/EOF paths in readTag/readLength/read(int), long-form length bounds in readLength (size > 4 / length >= limit), indefinite-length handling (readLength returns -1), or the seq size != 2 check in asn1derToConcatenatedRS. These are specific, diff-grounded missing tests for nontrivial parsing logic, but not a directly verifiable runtime defect by themselves.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java:53 — Coverage depends on one random signature per algorithm, with no fixed vectors for r/s that have leading zero bytes (short DER INTEGER) or a set high bit (0x00 sign byte), so these branches are hit only by chance.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` signs fixed data but uses Java ECDSA `Signature`, which produces randomized signatures; it then round-trips DER<->(r||s) and asserts equality. This validates basic symmetry but does not deterministically exercise edge cases in the newly added ASN.1 integer handling (e.g., DER INTEGER needing a leading 0x00 when the high bit is set, or trimming/expanding when `BigInteger.toByteArray()` yields a shorter/longer representation). Those branches in `AuthzClientCryptoProvider.integerToBytes(...)` and the DER encode/decode paths would only be hit by chance without fixed vectors/crafted r/s values.

adjudication_records.issue_text: common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java:57 — Nothing tests the change from failing on "multiple providers" to picking by order; Default/Elytron/FIPS all return 200, so a tie is now silently decided by ServiceLoader order and never checked.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to no longer throw when multiple CryptoProvider implementations are present; instead it sorts by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and returns the first provider, logging the rest. However, the diff also sets DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider to all return the same order (200), so in the common case of multiple providers on the classpath the selection is still ambiguous and will be determined by ServiceLoader iteration order, with no tie detection/error. This is a real behavioral change from deterministic failure to potentially nondeterministic provider choice.

adjudication_records.issue_text: authz/client/src/main/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/AuthzClient.java:95 — No test checks that AuthzClient.create runs CryptoIntegration.init and resolves AuthzClientCryptoProvider through META-INF/services; the test creates the provider directly, so the service registration and order (100 vs 200) are unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new behavior in `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` to call `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` and introduces an SPI registration file `authz/client/src/main/resources/META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider` pointing to `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, plus new provider selection logic in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` (sorted by `CryptoProvider::order`). The only added test (`ECDSAAlgorithmTest`) instantiates `new AuthzClientCryptoProvider()` directly and does not exercise `AuthzClient.create(...)`, `CryptoIntegration.init(...)`, or `ServiceLoader` resolution/ordering (e.g., `order()` 100 vs other providers at 200). This is a concrete, diff-grounded missing test for the newly added integration path, but not a proven functional defect by itself.
